title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers used AI-generated video and text to impersonate a real immigration attorney on social media, creating hundreds of fake profiles across multiple platforms. The impersonation deployed AI as a tool for fraud rather than as a system failure by a developer or deployer. The criminals generated deepfakes and fake promotional content claiming to offer immigration services at specific prices, then directed victims to make payments through informal channels while providing fraudulent contracts.

This shows the vulnerability of identity-based services to synthetic media impersonation at scale. The fraud targeted a specific, named individual whose reputation and expertise made him a credible-seeming service provider, which scammers could copy cheaply across platforms. A human verification step, such as confirming a lawyer's identity through bar association databases before payment, would have prevented financial loss.

It is not established who created or deployed the AI system, what specific generative tools were used, or whether the platforms had any way to detect the impersonation before the attorney reported it.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos featuring Leal promoting immigration services he never offered, including false claims about obtaining US residency for $2,200. The fraud escalated dramatically over the past three months, with scammers directing victims through WhatsApp to send money via payment apps like Venmo and Zelle while providing fake contracts and testimonials.

After learning about the scheme when suspicious callers contacted his office, Leal hired an anti-piracy company that removed approximately 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of social media advertisements requesting immediate payment for immigration benefits.
